text:
Temporal modeling challenges a fixed “protect the latest two items” heuristic: equal positional distances can represent hours or months. [TiSASRec](https://jiachengli1995.github.io/files/wsdm20.pdf) established jointly learned attention using historical pairwise time intervals and positions; its temporal mechanism is relevant without adopting its causal backbone. [TemProxRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09784) combines absolute/relative temporal and positional embeddings with contrastive learning, distinguishing within-user interaction spacing from contemporaneous behavior across users. These findings motivate testing learned temporal relevance, but do not establish gains for this Amazon benchmark.

A compatible experimental hypothesis is one BERT4Rec network with per-head attention biases indexed by clipped, logarithmically bucketed historical time gaps, optionally retaining interval direction. Preserve bidirectional masked-item training and appended-mask inference. For the appended mask, use a learned unknown-time relation; alternatively, encode each observed item’s age relative to the latest observed interaction. Both avoid supplying the next interaction’s timestamp. Apply the same rule to supervised masked positions during training so their actual timestamps cannot become a shortcut. This is a proposed adaptation, not a directly validated recipe from the cited papers.

Evaluate against position-only BERT4Rec and the latest-two heuristic using fixed macro validation HR@10, keeping one jointly trained checkpoint per category. Inspect performance across history lengths and interval variability. Avoid interpreting attention weights alone as proof of interest drift: a [2026 temporal-attribution benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27201), including BERT4Rec, found raw attention unreliable and gradient-based attribution more faithful. Temporal spacing is an observable signal; latent intent changes remain a hypothesis.
